title: SpaceX Is About to Catch a Spaceship With Chopsticks
paragraphs: Imagine throwing your phone high into the air, and catching it with a pair of chopsticks. Now make the phone a rocket. A really, really big one. That is basically what SpaceX does with its giant Super Heavy booster.
But this week, SpaceX wants to try something no one has ever done. Catch both halves of the rocket. The booster, and the spaceship on top. The ship has never been caught. Not once.
SpaceX calls it the first full recovery of an orbital launch system. So how do you catch a spaceship falling out of space? And why would anyone even try?

The launch is set for Friday, November thirteenth. Yes, Friday the thirteenth. Liftoff is planned from Starbase, in South Texas, at five forty-five p.m. Eastern, with a seventy-five minute window. And it still needs a final green light from the FAA.
The rocket has two parts. At the bottom is Super Heavy, the booster. On top is Starship, the ship. A couple of minutes after liftoff, the two halves split apart.
The booster flips around and heads back toward the launch site. It steers itself all the way back to the tower it launched from. Then it fires its engines one last time, to slow down.
And the tower grabs it, with two giant arms. Fans call them the chopsticks. The tower itself has a nickname too. Mechazilla. The whole trip back takes less than seven minutes.
SpaceX first pulled this off in October, twenty twenty-four. And it worked on the very first try.

Meanwhile, the ship keeps going, all the way to orbit. It will circle the Earth about fourteen times, around one hundred seventy miles up. Along the way, it will release twenty-six new Starlink internet satellites.
Then it waits. For almost a whole day. Ground teams use that time to check that every system is healthy. About twenty-two and a half hours after launch, it comes home.
This is the hard part. The ship hits the atmosphere belly first, falling sideways, like a skydiver. It uses its flaps to steer.

Then, close to the ground, it relights its engines. It swings itself upright. And it slows down, until it settles right between the chopsticks. The arms close. And, if everything goes right, the ship is caught.
But if anything looks wrong, SpaceX says the ship will not come home at all. Instead, it will be sent down into the ocean, far from people.
So why not just let rockets fall into the sea, like we used to? Because throwing away a rocket is like throwing away a plane after one flight.
If you can catch it, you can check it, fix it, and fly it again. That could make launches cheaper, and a lot more frequent. Elon Musk called it a profound technology milestone.
This did not happen overnight. The last flight, in late September, reached orbit for the first time. But a problem cut the mission short, and the ship splashed down in the Pacific.
Now SpaceX thinks it is ready for the full trick. The booster has been caught before. The ship never has.

So on Friday the thirteenth, watch the tower. Two catches. One rocket. And, if it works, nothing left floating in the ocean. If it doesn't, the ship ends up in the sea, and the engineers go back to work.
Remember the phone and the chopsticks? This time, SpaceX is trying to catch two of them. And one is falling from space. Do you think they'll catch both? Tell me in the comments.
